assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars. That is what money buys now.

Stocks grow 5.0% a year above inflation on average, and bonds 1.8%. Some years are good and some are bad. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They stay fixed, so every plan faces the same markets. To see a bad stretch, try 'markets fall 30%'.
A market test is one made-up run of the markets, year by year. We test many of them. 'Safe in 90 of 100 market tests' means your money lasts in 90 of every 100.

Until you retire you save about $63,832 a year. $20,500 goes into a 401(k) or IRA: that is assumed, 10% of pay. $43,332 is take-home pay left after spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays the same until you retire. The plan counts no raises, since they are not certain. If your pay changes, update it in your answers.
Your retirement spending leaves out the mortgage. Payments after you retire, until 2031, are a separate cost.

Social Security is a rough guess from today's pay. We count work from about 22 until you retire. Missing years under 35 count as zero. Your own figure is at ssa.gov/myaccount. Your answers show $77,800 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 69 for each of you. That pays about $90,200 a year.
A partner with little pay gets half of the other's benefit at 67. It is less if started sooner.
After the first death, the one left keeps the larger Social Security check, about $53,400 a year. Spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.
If you retire before 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until Medicare starts. This is a guess. Other health costs follow US government figures by age.

Tax uses 2027 federal rates, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving lowers your taxable pay. The child tax credit applies. In retirement we count 85% of Social Security as taxed. That is the most the law allows, so tax may run a little high. Your state taxes part of it too.
The plan runs until your partner is 94. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long. This comes from a US life table. People with more money often live longer.

worth_checking.title: Term life insurance
worth_checking.why: People depend on your pay, and you have no life cover. Term life pays your household if you die while you still work. This is something to look into, not a recommendation. I have not priced it.

It keeps your needs safest and leaves the most to spend. Few example households are like yours, so treat this as a rough guide.

rows.title: A poor first decade
rows.what: Stocks earn 5 points a year less than usual for the first 10 years of your retirement.
rows.label: Stocks do badly for 10 years
rows.short: Savings run out when you are 96. You would cut about $21,000 a year for 8 years.
rows.sentence: Your $82,000 a year still lasts in most market tests. In the worst 1 in 10, savings run out when you are 96. You would then cut about $21,000 a year for 8 years.

rows.title: The first death comes 10 years early
rows.what: The first of you to die does so 10 years sooner than expected. After that you get one Social Security check, and spending falls to 75%.
rows.note: Spending falls as well, so the money goes a little further. The one who is left has less income.
rows.label: The first death comes 10 years early
rows.sentence: The plan still works. You could still spend about $82,000 a year. Spending drops to 75% for the one left.

rows.title: You both live 10 years longer together
rows.what: The first death comes 10 years later than expected. The two of you spend at the higher level for longer.
rows.note: Two Social Security checks also last longer, and they more than pay for it.
rows.label: You both live 10 years longer together
rows.sentence: The plan still works. You could still spend about $82,000 a year.
